title: Checkpoint 6 Maths: The Test and How to Prepare
kicker: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint · Mathematics 0096 · Stage 6 · Start here
summary: How the Cambridge Primary Checkpoint Mathematics test works — papers, marks, calculator rules, mark-scheme words and results — plus a study plan and Thinking and Working Mathematically explained.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: This course follows the Cambridge Primary Mathematics curriculum framework (0096) for Stage 6: all 54 content objectives in three strands — Number; Geometry and Measure; Statistics and Probability.
It also builds the eight characteristics of Thinking and Working Mathematically (TWM.01–TWM.08), which run through every topic rather than being a separate chapter.
Every lesson page starts with a box like this one that lists its objectives and their codes (for example 6Ni.01), so students, parents and teachers can see exactly what is covered.

blocks.text: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint is taken at the end of Cambridge Primary. It tests the skills, knowledge and understanding a student should have at the **end of Stage 6**. This page explains how the Mathematics test works, what the examiners look for, and how to use this free course to get ready — step by step.

blocks.caption: Checkpoint Mathematics: two papers of 45 minutes, 40 marks each.

items: **Equipment:** the paper covers list compasses and a protractor, with tracing paper as optional. You also need your pens and an HB pencil, and a calculator for Paper 2.

**Pen and pencil:** write answers in black or dark blue pen. Use an HB pencil for diagrams and graphs. Do not use erasable pens or correction fluid — if you make a mistake, cross it out neatly and write the new answer next to it.
**Working:** show all your working in the booklet, in the space next to the question.
**Size of the papers:** recent papers have been about 20 pages long, with roughly 30 numbered questions. Most questions are worth **1 mark**; a few are worth **2 marks**.
**When:** from 2026 Cambridge runs Checkpoint in three series a year — March, May and October — on a fixed timetable. Your school will tell you which series and dates apply to you.

blocks.title: Older past papers
blocks.text: You may find past papers with the code **0845**. They were written for the previous curriculum. They are still useful practice, but papers with the code **0096** match the current framework that this course follows.

There is no separate multiple-choice section. Short "choose" questions (tick, ring, match) are mixed in with questions where you write your own answer. Here are the styles you will meet — every lesson in this course practises them.

rows: Write a number in the answer box or space
Draw a ring around, or tick, the correct answer(s)
Ring the two numbers that are multiples of 6.
Tick a box and give a reason
Is 0.5 bigger than 0.45? Explain how you know.
A position–term table for a sequence
Match each fraction to its percentage.
Write numbers or shapes in a Venn or Carroll diagram
Plot points, draw a reflection, rotation or translation, construct a circle
Reflect the triangle in the mirror line.
Take values from a bar chart, line graph, pie chart…
How many more…? What was the temperature at 2 pm?
Fill in boxes, or write <, > or =
Complete a column method or grid
Fill in the missing digits in a long multiplication.

blocks.text: **Timing:** 45 minutes for 40 marks is just over 1 minute per mark. A 1-mark question should not take you 5 minutes. If you are stuck, mark it in the margin, move on, and come back at the end.

The papers are marked by Cambridge using a **mark scheme**. Each row of the mark scheme gives the question, the correct answer, the marks, any **part marks**, and **guidance** for the examiner. Knowing the short codes helps you understand why working matters.

rows: You get a mark for a correct method, even if the final answer is wrong — so write the method down.
A mark for the correct answer. It usually depends on a correct method.
A mark for a correct answer or statement on its own.
If you got part (a) wrong but used your answer correctly in part (b), you can still get the mark for (b).
Other correct forms are accepted, e.g. ½, 0.5 or 2/4.
Only that exact answer earns the mark — no other form, no part credit.
Once the correct answer is seen, later extra work is ignored.
A step earns credit if it is written, or clearly used in your working.
This mark can only be given if an earlier mark was given.
A mark given for a particular partly correct answer described in the scheme.
The answer only scores if it did not come from incorrect working.

blocks.text: Typical examiner guidance says things like "award 1 mark for a complete correct method with arithmetic errors" or "if any arithmetic is shown, it must be correct". So on 2-mark questions, **always show your working**: a clear method can earn 1 mark even if you slip at the end. But keep the working neat and correct — wrong extra working can cost you.

blocks.title: "Show your working" — what to write
items: Write the calculation you are doing, not just the answer: 3 × 28 = 84, then 100 − 84 = 16.
Number lines, tables, bar models and sketches count as working.
Put your final answer where the question asks (in the box or on the line), with units if needed.
If you change your mind, cross out the wrong work with one neat line so the examiner can see your new answer.
Students receive a **statement of achievement**.

Schools receive a **diagnostic feedback report**, showing strengths and weaknesses. Results are reported for the subject as a whole and for each **strand** (Number; Geometry and Measure; Statistics and Probability).
Results also give schools an **international benchmark** for their students' performance.

blocks.text: Because results are reported by strand, a gap in one area (for example Statistics) shows up clearly. This course is arranged by strand so that you can fix weak areas one at a time.

Every lesson page has the same shape: **In the curriculum** → key words (with Arabic) → teaching with diagrams → **worked examples** → common mistakes and **How Checkpoint asks this** → an interactive **practice quiz** with full solutions → **Remember** summary.

items: Read the teaching sections and copy the key words and rules into a maths notebook.
Cover each worked example's solution, try it yourself, then compare line by line.
Do the practice quiz without a calculator unless it says calculator allowed. Use paper for working, exactly as in the real test.
Write every question you got wrong into an **error log**: the question, your mistake, the correct method.
One week later, redo the quiz. Aim for full marks before you move on.
After each strand, do a mixed review; at the end, do the three full practice tests in timed conditions (45 minutes per paper).

rows: Know the test, set up your notebook and error log
Negative numbers, sequences, order of operations, ×, ÷, factors, squares and cubes
Number: place value, decimals, fractions, percentages and ratio (8 pages)
Most of Paper 1 and Paper 2 use these skills
Bring compasses, protractor and a ruler
Reading and drawing graphs; averages; probability words
Timed: Paper 1 without a calculator, Paper 2 with one; mark using the solutions

blocks.text: This is a suggestion — two lesson pages a week fits well around school. If your test is sooner, do one page a day and spend the extra time on your weakest strand.

blocks.title: لولي الأمر
items: امتحان Checkpoint رياضيات = ورقتين، كل ورقة 45 دقيقة و40 درجة. الورقة الأولى بدون آلة حاسبة، والثانية مسموح فيها بالآلة الحاسبة.
الطالب بيجاوب في ورقة الأسئلة نفسها، ولازم يكتب خطوات الحل لأن في درجات على الطريقة (method marks).
النتيجة بتطلع شهادة للطالب وتقرير للمدرسة يوضح المستوى في كل فرع (الأعداد – الهندسة والقياس – الإحصاء والاحتمالات).
أفضل طريقة: صفحتين في الأسبوع، وكراسة أخطاء يكتب فيها الطالب كل سؤال غلط فيه ويعيد حله بعد أسبوع.

blocks.text: Cambridge wants you not only to calculate, but to **think like a mathematician**. There are eight characteristics, in four pairs. You will not see the words "specialising" or "conjecturing" in a test question, but you will see questions such as "Explain how you know", "Give an example to show this is wrong", "Sort these numbers" and "Describe the pattern" — those are TWM.

blocks.caption: The eight TWM characteristics come in four pairs.

rows: Try a particular example to test an idea
Is the sum of three numbers in a row always a multiple of 3? Try 4 + 5 + 6 = 15 ✓ and 10 + 11 + 12 = 33 ✓.
Spot the pattern that works for all the examples
"The sum of three numbers in a row is always 3 × the middle number."
Make a guess or ask a "what if…?" question
"I think two odd numbers always add to an even number." "What if I add four numbers in a row?"
Give evidence to prove an idea — or one example to show it is wrong
"All numbers ending in 4 are multiples of 4" is wrong: 14 ÷ 4 = 3.5.
Describe the mathematical properties of something
A square: 4 equal sides, 4 right angles, 2 pairs of parallel sides, 4 lines of symmetry, rotational symmetry of order 4.
Sort things into groups by their properties
Put 6, 9, 12, 14, 15 into a Venn diagram for "even" and "multiple of 3".
Compare methods or answers; find advantages and disadvantages
For 8 × 49: column method vs 8 × 50 − 8. The second is quicker in your head.
Make a method or diagram better
Change a messy list of pairs that add to 10 into an organised table, so no pair is missed.

blocks.text: **A TWM example in action.** Look at 1 + 3 = 4, 1 + 3 + 5 = 9, 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16. **Specialising:** we tried three cases. **Conjecturing:** "I think adding the first few odd numbers always gives a square number." **Generalising:** the first 5 odd numbers should give 5 × 5 = 25 — check: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 25 ✓. **Convincing:** the dot diagram of a square grows by an L-shape of an odd number of dots each time.

items: Read every question twice. Underline the key words: **estimate**, **explain**, **show**, **nearest**, **units**, **two**.
If a question says "Tick two" or "Ring all", count how many you have given.
Write the units (cm, cm^{2}, kg, °C) when the answer line does not already show them.
On Paper 1, use quick written methods and number facts; on Paper 2, use the calculator but still write the calculation you typed.
Estimate before you calculate, then check your answer is sensible.
For "Explain" questions write a full sentence with a number fact, e.g. "No, because 7 × 7 = 49 and 8 × 8 = 64, so 50 is not a square number."
Use a sharp HB pencil and a ruler for drawings; draw points and lines accurately.
Leave no question blank — a sensible attempt or a method can still score.

blocks.title: Common mistakes in Checkpoint Maths
items: Answering a different question: giving the total when it asks for the difference, or the area when it asks for the perimeter.
Only writing an answer on a 2-mark question, with no method — a slip then scores 0 instead of 1.
Forgetting "to the nearest…" or "give your answer as a fraction".
Spending too long on one hard question and not finishing the paper.
Using the calculator for everything on Paper 2 and typing it wrongly — always ask: is my answer about the right size?
Writing the answer in pencil or using correction fluid.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks TWM
items: "Explain how you know." → give a reason with numbers (Convincing).
"Give an example to show that … is not correct." → one counter-example (Specialising/Convincing).
"Sort these numbers/shapes into the diagram." → Classifying.
"Describe the pattern" / "What is the 20th term?" → Generalising.
"Which method is better? Why?" or "Explain the mistake" → Critiquing.

blocks.title: Know your test
blocks.intro: 8 quick questions about the Checkpoint test and Thinking and Working Mathematically.

questions.q: How many minutes is each Checkpoint Mathematics paper?
questions.e: Each paper (Paper 1 and Paper 2) lasts 45 minutes.

questions.q: In which paper are you allowed to use a calculator?
questions.e: Paper 1 is the non-calculator paper. A calculator is allowed in Paper 2.

questions.q: In a mark scheme, what does "oe" mean?
questions.e: oe = or equivalent: other correct forms (for example ½, 0.5 or 2/4) are accepted.

questions.q: In a 2-mark question, you write a correct method but make a small adding mistake, so your final answer is wrong. What will you most likely get?
c: 0 marks, because the answer is wrong
2 marks, because the method is right
You lose a mark from another question
questions.e: Two-mark questions usually give a method mark (M1) for a correct method even when the final answer is wrong. That is why you should always show your working.

questions.q: Hana wants to check the statement "Every multiple of 4 is even." She tries 12, 20 and 36. Which TWM characteristic is she using?
questions.e: Choosing particular examples to test whether they meet a rule is specialising (TWM.01).

questions.q: Youssef sorts a set of shapes into a Carroll diagram: "has a right angle / does not have a right angle" and "quadrilateral / not a quadrilateral". Which TWM characteristic is this?
questions.e: Organising objects into groups by their properties is classifying (TWM.06). (Describing the properties of one shape would be characterising.)

questions.q: Continue the pattern (generalising). What is the total of the first 10 odd numbers, 1 + 3 + 5 + … + 19?
questions.e: The first 2 odd numbers add to 2 × 2 = 4, the first 3 to 3 × 3 = 9, the first 4 to 4 × 4 = 16. So the first 10 odd numbers add to 10 × 10 = 100. (Check by pairing: 1 + 19 = 20, 3 + 17 = 20, … 5 pairs × 20 = 100 ✓)

questions.q: Sami says: "All numbers that end in 4 are multiples of 4." Give an example to show that Sami is wrong, and explain.
questions.ms: 1 mark: a correct counter-example with a reason, e.g. 14 (14 ÷ 4 = 3.5, not a whole number), or 34, 54, 74, 94… Accept any number ending in 4 that is not a multiple of 4, with working or a reason. Do not accept 4, 24, 44, 64, 84 (these are multiples of 4).
questions.e: Example: 14 ends in 4, but 14 ÷ 4 = 3.5, which is not a whole number, so 14 is not a multiple of 4. One counter-example is enough to show a statement is false (convincing, TWM.04).

blocks.title: Remember
items: Two papers, 45 minutes and 40 marks each. Paper 1: no calculator. Paper 2: calculator allowed.
Answer on the paper in black or dark blue pen; diagrams in HB pencil; no correction fluid.
Show your working — 2-mark questions often give a method mark.
Results are reported for the subject and for each strand, so work on your weakest strand.
Think like a mathematician: test examples, spot patterns, explain, sort, compare and improve (TWM).
Use every lesson page fully: worked examples → quiz → error log → redo.
